segments.speaker: CLARE
segments.en: Hi Jake. How are you getting on with the practical teaching?

segments.speaker: JAKE
segments.en: It’s harder than I expected, but I’ve got some great classes. How about you?

segments.speaker: CLARE
segments.en: Not brilliant. I’m really struggling with my Year 12 science class.

segments.speaker: JAKE
segments.en: Are they hard to control?

segments.speaker: CLARE
segments.en: Well, I don’t have discipline problems as such. It’s just that they don’t seem to think that science has anything to do with their lives. It’s depressing. They listen to what I say, and I gave them a test last week and the results weren’t too bad, but there’s no real engagement.

segments.speaker: JAKE
segments.en: Right.

segments.speaker: CLARE
segments.en: And as part of my teaching practice, I have to design an experiment for them to do. I was wondering about something on the children’s diets... you know, asking them to record what they eat and maybe linking it to their state of health.

segments.speaker: JAKE
segments.en: Mmm. Let’s think. So your methodology would involve the children recording what they eat. OK, but you’d also need to have access to the children’s medical records and I don’t think people would be happy about that; confidentiality would be an issue. If you could get the right data, the conclusions might be significant, but I suspect it’s just not going to be easy.

segments.speaker: CLARE
segments.en: Right.

segments.speaker: JAKE
segments.en: Have you thought about doing an experiment using animals?

segments.speaker: CLARE
segments.en: Wouldn’t that be upsetting for the children?

segments.speaker: JAKE
segments.en: Well, the animals don’t have to be harmed in any way. It could just be an experiment where they’re given a certain diet and the effects are observed.

segments.speaker: CLARE
segments.en: Would I have to get permission to use animals?

segments.speaker: JAKE
segments.en: Yes, you’d have to submit an outline of the experiment and fill in a form, but it’s quite straightforward.

segments.speaker: CLARE
segments.en: But if we found out that, say, a particular diet affects the health of animals, the same thing wouldn’t necessarily be true for people, would it?

segments.speaker: JAKE
segments.en: No that’s true, but the findings for any experiment are going to be limited. It’s inevitable.

segments.speaker: CLARE
segments.en: I suppose so. So what animals could I use to investigate the effects of diet? Mice?

segments.speaker: JAKE
segments.en: Yes. You’d need experimental mice – ones that have been specially bred for experiments. OK, so what will your experiment be investigating exactly?

segments.speaker: CLARE
segments.en: Well, something to do with nutrition. So maybe we could look at food supplements... things like extra iron and extra protein, and their impact on health.

segments.speaker: JAKE
segments.en: Mmm. That might be rather broad. Maybe just look at the effects of one supplement, like sugar, on the health of the mice?

segments.speaker: CLARE
segments.en: In fact, maybe the focus could be on whether mice can control their own diet.

segments.speaker: JAKE
segments.en: So, what happens when they have access to more sugar, that they don’t really need?

segments.speaker: CLARE
segments.en: Exactly. Do they eat it or do they decide to leave it?

segments.speaker: JAKE
segments.en: Great. Then later on, you could do a follow-up experiment adding another variable. Like, you could give some of the mice the chance to be more active, running on a wheel or something, and the others just sit around and don’t do much.

segments.speaker: CLARE
segments.en: Or I could repeat the experiment but change the type of food I provided . . . or use mice with a different genetic structure. But I think your idea would be more interesting, I might think about that some more.

segments.speaker: CLARE
segments.en: So can I talk through a possible procedure for the experiment where mice are given a sugar supplement?

segments.speaker: JAKE
segments.en: Sure. I did a similar experiment in college actually.

segments.speaker: CLARE
segments.en: Great. So how many mice would I need?

segments.speaker: JAKE
segments.en: I’d say about 12. And all young ones, not a mixture of old and young.

segments.speaker: CLARE
segments.en: OK. And I’d need two groups of equal sizes, so six in each group. And how would I tell them apart? I suppose I could put some sort of tag on one group... or just mark them in some way?

segments.speaker: JAKE
segments.en: You could use food colouring, that wouldn’t hurt them.

segments.speaker: CLARE
segments.en: Perfect. Then each group would go into a separate cage, and one group, let’s call them group A, would be the control group. So they’d just have ordinary mouse food. I suppose you can buy that?

segments.speaker: JAKE
segments.en: Yes, it comes in dry pellets.

segments.speaker: CLARE
segments.en: And the other group would have the same as the first group, but they’d also have the extra sugar.

segments.speaker: JAKE
segments.en: Would you just give them straight sugar?

segments.speaker: CLARE
segments.en: I might be better to give them something like cereal with it.

segments.speaker: JAKE
segments.en: Hmm. Then you’d need to weigh the mice, I should think once a week. And you’d need an electronic balance.

segments.speaker: CLARE
segments.en: But we can’t hold them on the balance, or it’d affect the reading.

segments.speaker: JAKE
segments.en: Exactly. So you need something called a weighing chamber to stop the mice from running away. It sounds complicated, but actually you can just use a plastic box with holes in the top.

segments.speaker: CLARE
segments.en: OK. So once we’ve measured the weight gain of each mouse we can work out the average for each group, as well as the standard deviation. And then see where we go from there. That sounds cool, I think the students will enjoy it.

segments.speaker: JAKE
segments.en: Yes. One thing...

SECTION 3
Questions 21-30
SCIENCE EXPERIMENT FOR YEAR 12
Choose the correct letter A, B or C.
Questions:
    Q Num: 21
    Text: How does Clare feel about the students in her Year 12 science class?
    Options:
        worried that they are not making progress.
        challenged by their poor behaviour in class.
        frustrated at their lack of interest in the subject.
    Q Num: 22
    Text: How does Jake react to Clare's suggestion about an experiment based on children's diet?
    Options:
        He is concerned that the results might not be meaningful.
        He feels some of the data might be difficult to obtain.
        He suspects that the conclusions might be upsetting.
    Q Num: 23
    Text: What problem do they agree may be involved in an experiment involving animals?
    Options:
        Any results may not apply to humans.
        It may be complicated to get permission.
        Students may not be happy about animal experiments.
    Q Num: 24
    Text: What question do they decide the experiment should address?
    Options:
        Are mice capable of controlling their food intake?
        Does an increase in sugar lead to health problems?
        How much do supplements of different kinds affect health?
    Q Num: 25
    Text: Clare might also consider doing another experiment involving
    Options:
        other types of food supplement.
        different genetic strains of mice.
        varying amounts of exercise.
